note: Historical and linguistic supplement only: four recommended substantive resources. Two optional classification-history works are preserved separately as supporting reading and excluded from the source count. Selected relevant passages were inspected, not entire books. No main data, site, or publication was changed.
minimumCountRecommendation: Four substantive works in sources. supportingReadingsNotCounted and optionalHistoricalContext are uncounted contextual notes, not additional resources for the published minimum.

sources.title: Historical Sketches of the Several Indian Tribes in Louisiana: Adaize account
sources.publisher: John Sibley; reprinted in American State Papers, Boston: Munroe, Francis, & Parker, 1808; scan from Internet Archive via Wikimedia Commons
sources.author: John Sibley
sources.annotation: 1805 account, communicated with Jefferson's 1806 message; inspected in a dated 1808 Boston reprint, printed pp. 42–44, especially the complete Adaize entry on p. 44 (PDF p. 52). Sibley distinguishes the community at Lac Macdon from the old Spanish establishment and describes multilingualism. His estimate concerns men, not the whole population. This is an official observer's account, containing judgments and secondhand claims; it is not an independently verified census or a tribal-authored history.

sources.title: A Report from Natchitoches in 1807
sources.publisher: Museum of the American Indian, Heye Foundation, Indian Notes and Monographs 25; Smithsonian Libraries / Internet Archive
sources.author: John Sibley; edited with an introduction by Annie Heloise Abel
sources.annotation: 1922 edition of Sibley's 1807 journal. Read the introduction's printed pp. 5–8 and August entries on pp. 49–56, especially August 13 on p. 50. Adai parties and chiefs appear among visitors receiving provisions. The August 18 formal council list on p. 56 does not name Adai, so the earlier visit must not be turned into a treaty-signature claim. The publication and its introduction reflect two different periods of outsider authorship.

sources.title: Source Material on the History and Ethnology of the Caddo Indians
sources.publisher: Smithsonian Institution, Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 132; full-text transcription hosted by the Louisiana Anthology
sources.author: John R. Swanton
sources.annotation: 1942 sourcebook. Inspected selected Adai passages on printed pp. 13–15, 21–23, 75, and 84–85. Swanton compares discrepant population estimates, reports Caddo recollections, and warns that a later village called Adaise cannot securely be identified as Indigenous. Its historical synthesis and quoted records require source-specific reading. His assertion that Adai were entirely merged with other Caddo is a dated author's conclusion, not a verdict on today's communities or their identities.

sources.title: Language Isolates of North America
sources.publisher: Routledge, in Language Isolates, pp. 193–228; author-posted full text on ResearchGate
sources.author: Marianne Mithun
sources.annotation: 2017 chapter, DOI 10.4324/9781315750026-8. Read the opening methodological discussion on printed pp. 193–195 and the Adai analysis on p. 195 in the author's publicly posted full text. Mithun explains documentation limits and argues that the surviving evidence suggests an isolate, citing Wallace Chafe's assessment. Use this for linguistic reasoning, not its compressed mission chronology. No claim is made to have inspected the underlying manuscript vocabulary or Chafe's unpublished communication.

proposedParagraphs.title: The people and the colonial place name
proposedParagraphs.text: Sibley's 1805 account describes an Adaize community at Lac Macdon, connected with the Bayou Pierre branch of the Red River. He explicitly places the old Spanish establishment some distance to its south and says it was named for the people. The passage therefore does not locate every Adai household inside the mission or presidio. It also describes long-standing residence, although that statement reaches readers through Sibley's account. Its demographic estimate is about twenty men with more women; it cannot be quoted as twenty people in total. Geographic distances, categories, and reported knowledge should remain attributed to this particular early United States observer.

proposedParagraphs.title: Multilingualism is different from language descent
proposedParagraphs.text: The same account says the Adai had a language of their own while also speaking Caddo and, in many cases, French. Those statements can coexist: using a neighboring language does not establish that one's ancestral language belongs to the same family. Mithun's 2017 discussion revisits the limited documentation and reports Chafe's rejection of identifying the recorded language as Caddo. She argues that an isolate is suggested, while explaining the broader difficulty of distinguishing an isolate from a language whose record is too limited to classify. This linguistic question should remain separate from contemporary Adai Caddo identity and the community's own reconstruction work.

proposedParagraphs.title: Adai visitors in the 1807 journal
proposedParagraphs.text: Sibley's separate 1807 journal records the arrival on August 13 of parties and chiefs from several named nations, including the Adaize. His entries discuss provisions, travel, horses, and relations with the United States agent. This is a useful record of named Adai presence within a network of neighboring communities after the earlier population estimate. It is also an administrator's selective account. The formal council list printed later in the journal does not name Adai; an earlier recorded visit should not be converted into a claim that Adai signed a particular treaty or attended every subsequent council session.

proposedParagraphs.title: Population tables and the persistence of names
proposedParagraphs.text: Swanton's 1942 sourcebook assembles estimates whose units vary between men, families, and total inhabitants. Its table even calculates some totals by multiplying warrior counts. These figures are evidence of what particular observers counted or estimated, rather than directly comparable modern censuses. Swanton also quotes land records using Adaes or Adaise and acknowledges uncertainty about the identity of a later village bearing that name. A place name alone cannot establish the inhabitants' identity or a complete genealogy. His further claim that Adai were entirely merged with other Caddo should be identified as his historical interpretation, rather than used to erase a present community's account of continuity.

integrationNotes: The community's programs page currently presents Caddoan affiliation as confirmed by several scholars. The inspected scholarship does not support an unqualified consensus claim: Powell expressly withholds a demonstration and Mithun argues for an isolate. Attribute each position and distinguish community identity from language genealogy.

Swanton's 1942 title is Source Material on the History and Ethnology of the Caddo Indians. Indian Tribes of the Lower Mississippi Valley and Adjacent Coast of the Gulf of Mexico is a separate 1911 book; it was located but not inspected substantively for this supplement and is not counted.

The Sibley 1805 source was read in an inspected 1808 Boston reprint, not the inaccessible original 1806 edition or the 1832 congressional compilation. Preserve that edition distinction and its correct printed page 44.
The 1805 historical sketch and 1807 journal are different primary documents. Reprints or quotations of the same 1805 sketch should not be counted again as independent resources.

Mission dates, royal administration, archaeology, and Los Adaes settlement history are being researched separately by the parent; no chronology from an older linguistic summary should override that work.

There are no reproduced ceremonial directions, precise burial locations, or claims to unrestricted rights in archival language material. Do not infer the extinction of a people from an ethnographer's inability to locate speakers.
researchGaps: Directly inspect and collate the surviving Adai manuscript vocabulary, its copy history, collector attribution, and date with the American Philosophical Society's actual holding before asserting an exact word count or original spelling.
Read Anthony P. Grant's 1995 conference paper, Allan R. Taylor's relevant 1963 publications, and any later specialist reassessment; metadata and citations alone were not counted here.
Compare the 1808 reprint with the 1806 edition and 1832 congressional printing, particularly where OCR or reprinting may distort dates and punctuation.

Community-authored institutional history and appropriately public family histories are required to connect nineteenth-century documents with current families; the material inspected does not establish individual genealogy or legal recognition.
Further work should distinguish the many uses of Adaes/Adaise in missions, civil settlements, land claims, and references to people, using dates and the author's stated subject in each document.

supportingReadingsNotCounted.title: Indian Linguistic Families of America, North of Mexico: Adaizan family
supportingReadingsNotCounted.publisher: Smithsonian Institution, Bureau of Ethnology, Seventh Annual Report, 1891; Project Gutenberg transcription
supportingReadingsNotCounted.author: John Wesley Powell
supportingReadingsNotCounted.annotation: Read the complete Adaizan discussion on printed pp. 45–47, including its bibliographic synonyms and qualification of Gatschet's proposed Caddoan relationship. Powell explicitly says sufficient evidence to establish that relationship was unavailable. His claims about disappearance, character, population, and early identification are period interpretations requiring independent checks. This optional work explains the history of classification; it is not present-day linguistic consensus or an independent modern community history.

supportingReadingsNotCounted.title: A Migration Legend of the Creek Indians, Volume I: Adai and Caddo discussions
supportingReadingsNotCounted.publisher: D. G. Brinton, Philadelphia, 1884; Project Gutenberg transcription
supportingReadingsNotCounted.author: Albert S. Gatschet
supportingReadingsNotCounted.annotation: Read the dedicated Adai section on printed pp. 41–42 and the following Caddo list on pp. 43–44, attributed to an unnamed Caddo speaker in 1882. Gatschet questions the older vocabulary's orthography while describing social affiliation. His manuscript attribution and broad linguistic suggestions require archival checking. This is optional evidence about an ethnographer's reasoning, not a second modern classification authority. Other peoples' migration narratives and ceremonial material are outside the inspected scope and proposed prose.

optionalHistoricalContext.title: How older classification proposals changed
optionalHistoricalContext.text: Gatschet's 1884 discussion distinguishes social affiliation from the surviving vocabulary and cautions that its spelling was unreliable. His following Caddo list, attributed to an 1882 speaker, includes Hadai among remembered divisions. Powell's 1891 account reports Gatschet's later comparison with Caddoan languages but expressly says that sufficient evidence to establish a relationship was unavailable. Reading the two works together shows why a proposed connection should not become a claim that classification was conclusively settled. Both are valuable records of nineteenth-century research, with dated assumptions and overlapping evidence; they do not replace current linguistic analysis or community testimony.
